faqs.q: There is a raccoon denning above my Chesterfield ceiling. Will you release it somewhere wild?
faqs.a: We cannot promise a release, because the state does not allow routine relocation — a captured raccoon must be destroyed or moved only under a separate department permit. What works in Chesterfield is getting the animal out and keeping the next one out: one-way eviction doors, removal under depredation rules where needed, and steel sealing at the roofline. Because raccoons lead SC Department of Public Health rabies results, we also treat attic contamination seriously and clean latrine spots rather than leaving them sealed in.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Chesterfield home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes we are called about in Chesterfield are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs around Sandhills farm center and Lynches River side of the county seat. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and the cottonmouth around wet ground, swamp edges, and pond banks. Identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, note where it went, and call us. Venomous snakes are safety-and-identification work, not a guaranteed capture, and the lasting fix is usually habitat — clearing brush, woodpiles, and rodent shelter near the house. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is referral-only — it is never handled as a removal job.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Chesterfield actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around Sandhills farm center and Lynches River side of the county seat: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my Pageland house. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Opossums den under houses because crawlspaces near watermelon-farm country and Lynches River bottoms in the county's west are dry, dark, and close to pet food and trash. One opossum is mostly a nuisance; a season of them brings droppings, torn insulation, and fleas. We trap the animal — opossums are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is not permitted in South Carolina — then screen vents and repair the crawlspace door so the shelter is gone, not just the tenant.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Pageland attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Pageland, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around watermelon-farm country and Lynches River bottoms in the county's west, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Pageland home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Pageland that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Pageland.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Pageland and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the watermelon-farm country and Lynches River bottoms in the county's west. Homeowners here phone us first about opossums under farmhouses, then about bats in older gables and church rooflines.

Small-town housing here mixes antebellum-era homes near the center with farmhouses and newer builds along the highways, nearly all with vented crawlspaces. Deep sand changes everything here: burrows hold their shape, armadillos and skunks dig easily, and longleaf pine woods press right up against farmyards and small-town lots.

Before we leave a Pageland home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: How do rats get into McBee homes?
faqs.a: Around McBee, rats follow food and cover: bird feeders, pet food, ivy and brush against the house, and the lines and limbs that reach the roof near Carolina Sandhills refuge edge and longleaf stands around town. The job is trapping inside, sealing every entry we find, and cutting the routes and food that drew them. We will show you the droppings and rub marks we used to confirm the species, because rat work fails when it is guessed at.

faqs.q: There are bats in my McBee attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In McBee we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near Carolina Sandhills refuge edge and longleaf stands around town, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my McBee house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a McBee job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Carolina Sandhills refuge edge and longleaf stands around town with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

Older farmhouses on pier foundations, small-town brick homes from the early 1900s, and scattered mobile homes on sandy lots make up most of the housing, with outbuildings on nearly every property. Between the pine stands and the creek bottoms, animals commute along fence rows and field drains, and sandy soil means a burrow opened one week is occupied again the next unless it is screened shut.

Every job in McBee ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Carolina Sandhills refuge edge and longleaf stands around town stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Jefferson attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Jefferson attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

Jefferson.wildlife_intro:
Our crew works Jefferson from the Lynches River swamp farms south of Pageland. The homes here sit in deep-sand longleaf Sandhills and refuge land west of the Great Pee Dee River swamps, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, gray squirrels, fox squirrels, armadillos account for the bulk of our Jefferson calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Farm-town and antebellum homes in the centers, with rural houses and farmsteads on sandy lots edged by longleaf and swamp. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Jefferson job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Chesterfield County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.
